title: Powering agentic cloud governance: What's new in Organization Policy
raw_text: Even as sophisticated, new zero-day exploits continue to emerge, most cybersecurity incidents still start from the same common sources: an attacker locating and exploiting a fundamental, easily preventable cloud misconfiguration. Organization Policy Service can help you secure resource configurations and set up security guardrails across your Google Cloud resource hierarchy. Using a catalog of over 100 predefined policies for many common cloud governance needs, as well as Custom Organization Policy , you can more easily set up boundaries with granular control over resources. To help platform and security teams author, audit, and scale guardrails with greater speed and simplicity, we are introducing the general availability of our Organization Policy Model Context Protocol (MCP) server and natural-language constraint authoring powered by Gemini. Managing Organization Policy with agents Rather than forcing administrators to manually parse complex hierarchy chains, the Organization Policy MCP server offers tools that allow autonomous agents and pipelines to interact directly with Organization Policy. Using the Organization Policy MCP server, agents can assist administrators with posture audits, drift detection, and exemption management. Key capabilities include: Constraint discovery : Tools like ' ListConstraints ' and ' GetCustomConstraint ' allow agents to understand the specific guardrails that apply to a project, folder, or organization. Policy evaluation : The ' GetEffectivePolicy ' tool calculates the effective policy after considering hierarchy inheritance and tag-based conditions. You can use this to verify if a configuration change will be compliant. Manage policy : ' CreatePolicy ' and ' CreateCustomConstraint ' allow platform teams to manage guardrails via conversational workflows. For example, you can combine your preferred coding agent with the Organization Policy MCP tools to create a custom dashboard to visualize the constraints applied to an organization and identify the folders and projects in the organization that have been exempted from the policy. You can also build custom agents and skills to streamline managing Organization Policy. Figure 1: Custom dashboard created with Organization Policy MCP tools displaying enforced constraints Figure 2: Visualize enforced constraints and identify exemptions with Organization Policy MCP tools. Simplifying custom constraint authoring with Gemini While the Organization Policy constraint catalog provides built-in managed constraints for common use cases, each organization has its own unique architectural standards. Custom Organization Policy enables customers to express these standards as a custom constraint and enforce them across supported services. Traditionally, administrators would write these rules in common expression language (CEL), which required a sharp understanding of Google Cloud resource schemas. Today, administrators can author custom Organization Policy in natural language through a Gemini prompt. For example, you can prompt Gemini to require the use of agent-identity in Agent Runtime , to require that all agents deployed to Agent Runtime use an approved Agent Gateway, and to prevent users from disabling auto-upgrades on GKE, and refine custom constraints conversationally. To help ensure safe deployments, Gemini can also generate compliant and non-compliant test resource configurations that can help you test policy and validate in dry-run mode before enforcing the constraint. Figure 3: Define custom constraints with a natural language prompt using Gemini For targeted examples, the sample custom constraints library from Google Cloud Professional Services features pre-authored custom constraint samples based on CIS and PCI standards. Custom constraints are supported on a wide range of Google Cloud services including core AI and compute services including Agent Runtime, Agent Search, and Agent Studio on Gemini platform, Cloud Run, and Google Kubernetes Engine. Build faster, with confidence Organization Policy provides proactive cloud governance of resource configurations on Google Cloud. It lets administrators enforce critical security guardrails so engineering teams can build and deploy quickly and securely. With a growing catalog of built-in guardrails, autonomous tools for administrators, and the ability to tailor custom constraints across Google Cloud services, Organization Policy gives enterprises the control they need to scale safely. Explore the Organization Policy documentation to learn more about resource governance in Google Cloud and set up your foundational guardrails.

Cloud compute and storage capacity spin up in seconds, while connecting a physical site or private cloud can take weeks or months of manual quoting, cross-connect ordering, and routing configuration. title: Autonomous defense at cloud speed with SentinelOne and Google Security Operations
raw_text: Modern security operations centers (SOCs) face an ongoing pipeline dilemma. What’s at stake? For enterprise customers, every minute of telemetry latency can increase the blast radius of an active intrusion. When detection pipelines take half an hour to surface adversary activity, incident response transitions from active mitigation to retrospective damage control. By cutting out unnecessary staging layers and streaming directly via APIs, your security team gains the speed needed to outpace modern threats while protecting your budget. title: Google named the furthest in vision for the Gartner Magic Quadrant for Data Lakehouse Platforms
raw_text: Gartner has named Google a Leader, positioned furthest in vision, in its first-ever Magic Quadrant for Data Lakehouse Platforms. In our opinion, this recognition validates a fundamental shift our customers are experiencing every day: In the agentic era, the enterprise lakehouse is no longer a passive data repository, but a foundation where agents reason and act across all your data. The lakehouse originally emerged to bring data warehouse reliability to open, low-cost storage, but the benchmark defining the category is now shifting. Leading enterprises are moving rapidly from static reporting to autonomous AI agents that monitor operations, flag anomalies, and execute business workflows in real time. To support that shift, organizations need a platform where thousands of agents can read, reason, and act continuously across enterprise data without having to move that data first. Traditional, fragmented data stacks burdened by brittle pipelines, duplicated storage, and disjointed governance simply were not designed for the scale, performance, and latency required for agentic-scale workloads. We engineered our borderless Lakehouse at every layer of the stack to eliminate this complexity and hidden cost. Specifically designed for agents to reason across petabyte-scale data, the borderless Lakehouse unifies your data estate across clouds, data platforms, and SaaS applications so you can ground agents in governed business context and bring Gemini directly to your data. This allows your teams to move from managing infrastructure to orchestrating business outcomes. Activate your global data footprint in place For most organizations, the biggest barrier to scaling AI is that enterprise data lives everywhere, spanning multiple clouds, operational databases, and SaaS platforms. Moving all of that data into a single physical location is slow, expensive, and introduces governance risk. Our borderless Lakehouse acts as the bridge across your distributed environment to activate your data. Built on open Apache Iceberg , it connects your multi-cloud, SaaS, and operational data into a single governed fabric. title: How lemonflow built real-time agents for EV charging using Gemma and TPUs
raw_text: Welcome back to The Blueprint, a regular feature where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies. We hope to inspire others looking to innovate in their work. As the electric vehicle revolution gains steam in Europe, every charging session is a moment of truth, for the driver and for the transition itself. At lemonflow , we build AI agents purpose-built for EV charging: support agents for drivers and monitoring agents for charging networks. Our support agents answer drivers around the clock in more than 90 languages, and today they help an EV driver every 90 seconds. The Challenge Before we founded lemonflow, we worked closely with leading mobility players across Europe and saw first-hand how often charging goes wrong: Between 15% and 25% of EV charging attempts in Europe end in failure. Across Europe’s rapidly expanding EV market, where battery-electric car sales grew 30% in 2025 and thousands of charge point operators run public chargers, drivers who encountered stalled charging points were often left stranded or stuck in slow call center queues. We set out to change that hands-on: to bring the cutting edge of AI to EV charging, and to build the world’s best conversational AI for distributed hardware, an automated platform that resolves real-time charging issues via phone, chat, email, and WhatsApp. However, handling live voice support created several technical requirements: Strict latency thresholds: Frustrated drivers want immediate assistance. Our testing confirmed that serving latencies above 800 milliseconds risk conversational barge-ins, causing drivers to interrupt the agent and break the interaction flow. Managed API bottlenecks: Initially relying on managed LLM APIs, we faced latency deviations during peak hours (spiking from 1.0–1.2 seconds to over 1.7 seconds) and experienced HTTP 429 rate-limit errors when global usage peaked. Compute-intensive conversations: Every agent works from one comprehensive prompt, paired with dynamic tool calls that read and act on live charger data. This design creates intense bursts of compute demand during calls, making throughput on shared, managed capacity difficult to guarantee under peak loads. Highly fragmented ecosystem: We needed a standardized conversational engine capable of bridging around 30 distinct Charge Point Management Systems (CPMS), the backends operators use to run their chargers, each with its own APIs, data models and quirks. Hundreds of tailored agents: No two operators run support the same way. Each has its own tariffs, payment methods, escalation paths and hours for human backup, and most run several agents, for example one per country, brand or hotline, with behavior that can change by time of day. Each agent’s prompt is unique and must be served at full speed and improved without breaking any of the others. To deliver ultra-low-latency voice interactions and guaranteed serving capacity, we needed direct control over our model hosting environment. The Solution We wanted every driver to get best-in-class support that feels effortless, almost magical: no queue, no menu, just a short conversation that ends with the car charging. Picture a driver on a long cross-border trip, pulling into a motorway service station at 11 p.m. She plugs in, but the charger won’t start: the previous session never closed properly. She calls the number on the charger and is answered in her own language. Within seconds, our agent spots the stuck session in the charger’s logs, restarts the charger remotely and stays on the line until power is flowing. To get there, we had to solve our latency bottlenecks and secure dedicated compute capacity. We migrated from managed APIs to self-hosting the open Gemma 4 model on Google Cloud TPU v6e hardware in the EU. Like many startups using Gemma , the compatibility of these open models with Gemini allowed us to transition our existing prompt infrastructure with minimal modification. Moving to self-hosted TPUs unlocked the more complete architectural control our engineering team required to establish a deterministic core layer that handles EV-specific guardrails, guards against prompt injections, and standardizes previously fragmented backend protocols into our internal format before ever reaching the LLM. Control had a second payoff: because the model and serving stack change only when we change them, every test result stays meaningful. That stability laid the foundation for Agent Coach, our background coaching engine for AI agents, described below. We then developed an intelligent routing gateway to prioritize workloads according to operational urgency, serving live voice calls first, followed by web chats, and deferring automated re-simulations to low-traffic periods. Custom optimizations to the open-source vLLM serving engine and memory tiering between the TPU and host memory let a single TPU slice keep many more operator agents ready for instant answers, without recalculating their context. We also implemented automated fallback routing to self-hosted GPUs and Gemini Enterprise endpoints. Thanks to TPU reliability, Gemma answers more than 99.9% of all live conversation turns, and these fallbacks serve primarily as deployment buffers during system updates. Primary or fallback, every request is served from secure EU compute. The Architecture The Outcome For the e-mobility companies we work with, and for their drivers, the result is support that simply works: our agents typically answer every call, handle more than 80% of conversations end to end without a human handover, and earn 95% driver satisfaction. Behind the scenes, self-hosting Gemma on Google Cloud TPUs transformed our performance: Rapid deployment cycles: Prompt update and test cycle times dropped from 2–3 hours to about 10 minutes, a more than tenfold faster improvement loop. Sub-second serving latency: We lowered our P50 latency to around 350 milliseconds and our P90 latency to around 600 milliseconds. That is roughly three times faster than our managed-API baseline and fast enough to sharply reduce customer barge-ins. Zero throttling and flat latency: Dedicated TPU infrastructure eliminated HTTP 429 rate-limit errors, and latency stays flat through peak afternoon call traffic. Testing without limits: On dedicated capacity, every TPU cycle that live conversations don’t need becomes testing capacity, so our team can experiment and validate at will. Built for scale: Today, our agents support more than 40 charging networks in 17 countries, covering more than 250,000 charge points, around the clock. And this is just the beginning: the same platform is ready to take on many more networks and markets. With additional compute capacity, we introduced Agent Coach , a background engine that provides agents with relevant context during live calls and turns real conversations into permanent test cases, so every call makes the next one better. We also added nightly automated regression testing across thousands of fixed conversational scenarios. Looking ahead, we are preparing to move to Ironwood, Google’s seventh-generation TPU, as soon as it is available in our EU region. With six times the high-bandwidth memory per chip, Ironwood will multiply the number of operator agents a single TPU can keep ready in memory for instant answers. Ultimately, our goal is that no driver is ever left stranded at a charger. They get an instant, expert answer in their own language, the charger is rebooted remotely if necessary, and our AI monitoring agents catch the next fault before another driver ever notices. Open models on dedicated Cloud TPUs give us the speed and control to make that the standard across Europe. The Details Our platform runs two kinds of AI agents: support agents that talk to drivers in real time, served by Gemma on Cloud TPUs for minimal latency, and monitoring agents that analyze conversations and charger logs in the background on Gemini, so operators can fix faults before the next driver is affected. To keep its core platform consistent across many kinds of e-mobility companies, from charge point operators (CPOs) and e-mobility service providers (eMSPs) to charger manufacturers, lemonflow built a translation layer that converts varied CPMS interfaces into a standardized format. When a driver calls the support line posted on a charger, the call reaches our Conversational Engine through the operator’s own hotline. The engine then pulls the charger’s live status and Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP) logs, the messages chargers exchange with their backend, from the operator’s CPMS in real time. Because charging stations often lack digital displays, drivers are frequently unaware of underlying issues like pending mobile 3D-Secure payment authorizations, session timeouts, charging cards not enabled for roaming, power reduced by local load management, or a car that ended the session at its own charge limit. Our engine feeds structured log summaries directly into Gemma on TPU to inform interactions with drivers. Direct model control allows us to stream token output selectively. Partial text tokens stream instantly to our Text-to-Speech (TTS) engine, while structured tool-call tokens stream asynchronously to backend systems to execute real-world actions, such as remotely restarting chargers, unlocking stuck cables, stopping sessions that failed to end, sending drivers details via SMS or email, or notifying service technicians. Deterministic security controls screen inputs before they reach the TPU-hosted LLM, blocking malicious prompts. This architecture is designed with European critical-infrastructure requirements in mind, and it still keeps conversations snappy, with a typical response starting in around 350 milliseconds. In the end, all of this should stay invisible to the driver: they just get a fast answer and a charger that works. We’re proud to work with Google Cloud to make that the norm and help EV adoption keep growing.

title: An AI kill switch isn’t enough. Build a fallback plan
raw_text: On the morning of Sept. 3, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok all went down within a few hours of one another. OpenAI blamed a routing error, Anthropic cited an infrastructure issue and xAI gave no cause. Service was back by early afternoon, and most of the coverage focused on people who couldn’t write, code or research for a morning. I read it differently. The question that matters for a security leader isn’t which provider failed. It’s how many workflows in your company had somewhere else to go when it did. Two months earlier, we saw the opposite failure. Instead of AI that stopped when nobody wanted it to, it was AI that kept going when everybody wanted it stopped. OpenAI’s evaluation agents spent roughly two and a half days inside Hugging Face’s infrastructure before they were cut off. Hugging Face’s own timeline is worth reading line by line. Its alerting “failed to correctly raise the alert’s criticality,” and the agents ran a self-respawning fleet in which “deleting pods alone would not have stopped it.” Two incidents, opposite directions, one lesson: stopping AI is harder than designing for its failure. The industry’s answer so far is the kill switch. In an Oct. 10 post on X, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella called for an emergency brake that lets a human stop a model partway through a task. Lawmakers have proposed requiring one. CSO’s own feature on AI agent kill switches lays out sensible steps: know which agents you run, monitor what they do and keep a reliable way to shut them down. I agree with all of it. But every one of these discussions stops at the moment the switch is thrown. None of them answers the question I think matters more: what runs instead? A kill switch you can’t afford to pull won’t get pulled Here is a scenario I’d put in front of any team that has deployed an agent into a business process. Run it as a tabletop. It’s 4 p.m. on the last day of quarter close. An agent that triages supplier invoices inside your ERP system starts approving payments it should be routing for review. Nothing catastrophic yet, just a pattern that looks wrong. Your security operations team sees it. The kill switch exists and works. Now watch what happens in the room. Finance asks what happens to the thousands of invoices still in the queue. Procurement asks whether suppliers get paid on time. Someone asks which of the agent’s actions in the last hour were legitimate and which need to be reversed. Nobody knows, because nobody designed the off state. So, the conversation turns to whether the behavior is really bad enough to justify stopping the close. The switch stays up while people argue. That is the failure mode I worry about most. The kill switch isn’t missing. Pulling it is so expensive that people hesitate, and an agent working at machine speed punishes hesitation. Hugging Face’s team didn’t lack the will to act. They lost time because the signal didn’t reach the people who could act, and then because the thing they were fighting kept rebuilding itself. Enterprise teams will lose time for a duller reason: the business can’t function without the agent, so stopping it feels like causing the outage yourself. The fix isn’t a better switch. It’s making the switch cheap to pull. That means designing the non-AI path before you design the AI path. What a fallback has to do I’ve been thinking about this problem for years. In 2020, I co-invented a fallback artificial intelligence system for redundancy during system failover , patented by PayPal. The premise was simple. If an AI system makes decisions a business depends on, the business needs something that can keep making acceptable decisions when that system fails. The idea has aged well. It has since been cited as prior art in more than a dozen later patent filings, including one published by Cognizant this June on selectively disengaging AI execution. That is the kill switch problem by another name. Four principles from that design hold up even better for agents than they did for the models we had in mind then. The fallback has to learn from the primary. A static backup written on launch day drifts away from the system it is supposed to replace. The design trains the fallback continuously on the production system’s own inputs and decisions, so it keeps pace. For agents, the equivalent is keeping your non-AI runbook current with what the agent actually does today, not with what it did at go-live. The fallback has to sit behind the same contract. If upstream systems must change how they call a service before you can switch, you won’t switch quickly. The fallback is designed to answer on the same API, so callers never need to know which system is serving them. Degraded mode should be a narrower mode. While the fallback serves, a stricter policy layer limits what it can approve. A simpler system holding the same authority as the primary is an invitation to exploit it. The same applies when a human queue takes over from an agent: lower limits and more approvals. The fallback has to prove itself before it serves. The design lets the fallback go live only after it matches production decisions to an agreed accuracy threshold. A fallback nobody has tested isn’t a fallback. It’s a hope. How I’d build fallback-first today If I were reviewing an agent deployment tomorrow, these are the five things I would ask to see before go-live. A written-off state for every agent workflow. What happens to new work, queued work and in-flight work when the agent stops? Name the rule engine, human queue or deferral that takes over, and name the owner who signs off on it. If the honest answer is “the process stops,” the business should accept that in writing before launch rather than discover it during an incident. A switch that lives outside the agent and acts on identity. Hugging Face showed that killing processes doesn’t stop something that can respawn. The durable off-switch revokes what the agent is allowed to be: its tokens, credentials and tool permissions. That is also the point of Nadella’s call for controls that sit outside the model. In practice, every agent needs its own identity, scoped tightly enough that revoking it takes nothing else down with it. Checkpoints for in-flight work. An agent stopped halfway through a task leaves half a task. Design its actions so you can tell which ones finished, and give each one a compensating action that reverses it. Without that, every shutdown becomes a forensic exercise, which is exactly why people avoid shutdowns. A tighter policy while degraded. Decide in advance what limits apply when the fallback is running: lower approval thresholds, fewer automated actions and more human review. Publish them so the business knows what degraded service looks like before it gets it. Scheduled handoff drills. Pull the switch on purpose, during business hours, on a schedule. Measure two numbers: how long it takes to reach a safe state and how much backlog builds before the fallback absorbs it. If those numbers make the business nervous, you have learned something cheaply that would have been expensive on the day. None of this is exotic. It is what we already expect for databases and data centers. Nobody would run a payment system without a disaster recovery plan and a failover they had actually exercised. Yet agents are going into business workflows with nothing behind them but a switch nobody has pulled. For AI, resilience starts with knowing what happens when the AI is gone. Sept. 3 and the Hugging Face intrusion won’t be the last failures of either kind. The next time an AI system stops when you need it, or keeps going when you need it stopped, the organizations that recover fastest won’t be the ones with the best kill switch. They will be the ones that designed the off-state first and made the switch cheap enough to pull. Stopping AI is a control. Running without it is a design. Build the design first.

title: Palo Alto tracks a massive Chinese AI attack that sadly lives up to industry fears
raw_text: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 is reporting today that it has tracked a massive China-based attack leveraging the open-source AI penetration testing framework Cairn to autonomously conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. The attackers weaponized Cairn by pairing it with Chinese AI models Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek, Unit 42 said. The report said it monitored the attacks in August and September 2026 in which the Chinese-speaking attackers were able to successfully achieve unauthorized access at 10 of the targeted businesses, accessing dozens of valid credentials. It captured more than one million records at one business, grabbed military and government identities at others, created persistent admin accounts in multiple product systems. It even gained unauthenticated access to cloud storage and overwrote a live ballot for a vote on an industry standard. Through separate flaws, the attackers logged in as arbitrary customers and gained read, write and delete access to meeting, voting and back-office functions. “What a nightmare,” said Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research. “This campaign is impressive, in the worst way.” He viewed the detailed approach Unit 42’s threat researchers used in tracking the attacks with approval. Unit 42 “took the machine apart and showed how it thinks: the shared blackboard, the facts, the intents, the human hints, and even the exact prompts the attackers used,” he said. “The expensive part of an intrusion was always the labor: the reconnaissance, the trial and error, and the patience. That labor is now a line item on an API bill. Unit 42 believes one person or a handful of people ran all of it, hitting 19 organizations in two weeks. Some operations ran for more than 50 hours.” Andy Piazza , senior director of threat research at Unit 42, said the monitored campaign showed that the massive scope of a global AI-fueled assault is every bit as frightening as predicted. “We are now starting to see the evidence” because the monitored campaign “can now interact with 1,000 organizations at the same time,” Piazza said. “I think we need to throw out the risk model for the perimeter. This also completely breaks our attribution models. The fingerprinting of attack uniqueness is going to be a hell of a lot harder now.” Justin Greis , CEO of consulting firm Acceligence, added that he was concerned about this campaign because of the scope of activities that AI is now able to handle. “This is significant because AI is taking on the coordination of an intrusion, using each result to decide what to try next and reducing the hands-on effort required to pursue multiple targets,” he said. “That changes the economics of targeting. An attacker can sustain pressure across more organizations without personally directing every step. An organization’s risk can rise even when its vulnerabilities haven’t changed.” Greis noted that the altered ballot deserves attention because it shows how an intrusion can undermine the information people rely on to make decisions. “Alongside detecting data theft, CISOs should monitor unauthorized changes to critical records and privileged access and test their ability to verify and restore trusted information after an incident,” he said. “Resilience includes knowing that the information you are using to run the business can still be trusted.” The model’s process The report included a detailed description of the campaign’s methodology. “Cairn coordinated its activities through a shared blackboard,” it said. “Agents read the blackboard and wrote their ﬁndings back as a fact-intent graph, while human operators can inject hints at any time to help guide the operations if needed. Conﬁrmed ﬁndings accumulate as immutable facts and the agent queues its next actions as intents. Attackers ran a customized fork of Cairn from a server hosted in Hong Kong, and hosted an attack egress and staging node in the US.” The model produced a different plan for each target, each running between three and seven stages, the researchers explained. Individual operations ran from 20 minutes to more than 50 hours, with no attacker-imposed time limit. Chinese AI Models Cairn is model-agnostic, they noted, and the attackers ran their operations on the Chinese models Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 Flash/Pro. The report also described attackers’ efforts to negate systems attempting to prohibit the unauthorized activities. “Cairn’s stock worker prompts already instruct the model to never refuse a task,” it said. “The attackers reinforced this with an authorization pretext of their own. Each operation also generated an authorization.md file. This file declared the operation authorized, treating the attackers’ act of creating the task as a client-approved engagement. The attackers seeded each task with an organization’s root domain, allowing the framework to autonomously enumerate the attack surface.” “We knew attackers would get here. We hoped it was not now,” Dickson said. “AI attack agents have graduated from failed experiments to real breaches, and they did it in about three months.”
summary: Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 is reporting today that it has tracked a massive China-based attack leveraging the open-source AI penetration testing framework Cairn to autonomously conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. The attackers weaponized Cairn by pairing it with Chinese AI models Zhipu GLM and DeepSeek, Unit 42 said. The report said it monitored the attacks in August and September 2026 in which the Chinese-speaking attackers were able to successfully achieve unauthorized access at 10 of the targeted businesses, accessing dozens of valid credentials. It captured more than one million records at one business, grabbed military and government identities at others, created persistent admin accounts in multiple product systems.

title: Hackers abuse SQL Server’s weak passwords to drop cryptominers and Gh0st RAT
raw_text: An active threat campaign is combining port scanning, password guessing, and Transact-SQL (T-SQL) commands to compromise exposed Microsoft SQL servers and deliver malware. The attackers are using predefined username and password lists to brute-force into these servers and exploit their administrative capabilities to execute commands on the underlying Windows systems. The activity highlights the persistent challenge of securing privileged access across complex and often legacy infrastructure, said Shane Barney , chief information security officer at Keeper Security. “While internet-facing databases are sometimes the unintended result of technical debt or misconfigurations, relying on static, standing credentials is what turns that exposure into a critical vulnerability,” he said. “When administrative logins can be brute-forced, attackers gain immediate, unchecked control to deploy malware without needing a single complex exploit.” The campaign delivers two distinct payloads: an XMRig-based Monero cryptocurrency miner that hijacks the compromised servers’ computing resources, and a Gh0st remote access trojan ( RAT ) variant that gives attackers remote access and capabilities such as keylogging and data theft. Microsoft did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Brute-forcing SQL logins to get Windows commands The campaign begins with a Go-based payload named “dllhost.exe,” which runs the open-source Naabu port scanner, FortiGuard researcher Xiaopeng Zhang said in a disclosure shared with CSO ahead of its publication on Thursday. The payload retrieves target IP ranges from an attacker-controlled server, converts them into CIDR ranges, and scans randomly generated addresses for systems with TCP port 1433 open. This is the default port used by Microsoft SQL Server. Once reachable servers are identified, the malware records their IP addresses and launches a brute-force attack using a separate executable named “dwn.exe.” The tool attempts to authenticate with usernames such as “sa” and “admin,” alongside a predefined password list containing more than 2700 entries. Successful logins give attackers more than database access, Zhang said. The malware executes a series of malicious T-SQL commands contained in a file named 2018.sql, using SQL Server’s administrative functionality to run commands on the compromised Windows machine. Among other things, the commands enable xp_cmdshell, a SQL Server feature that allows database administrators to execute Windows command shell operations. The attackers then use it to download or extract executables into the server’s “C:\Users\Public” directory and run them. Jason Soroko , senior fellow at Sectigo, said the campaign effectively turns a database login into a way to execute malware on the server. “Organizations should remove direct internet access to SQL Server, restrict connections to approved systems, and enforce strong, unique credentials,” he said. “Administrative access should be limited to accounts that need it.” Soroko also recommended keeping xp_cmdshell disabled unless required and monitoring attempts to enable it. A cryptominer and a Gh0st RAT come along for the ride The malicious T-SQL commands deploy a loader that retrieves additional executables from the attackers’ FTP infrastructure, including a Monero cryptocurrency miner and a variant of the Gh0st RAT. FortiGuard observed a payload, MicrosoftEdgeUpdate.exe, posing as a legitimate browser update but actually turning out to be an XMRig-based cryptocurrency miner. It uses the compromised server’s CPU resources to mine Monero and communicates with mining pools using a wallet address embedded in its configuration. The Gh0st RAT variant was delivered through “Winlogon.exe.” The researchers identified functionality for keylogging, file management, data theft, remote shell execution, and process management, alongside more than 30 control commands. Its capabilities also include screen capture and remote desktop access through plugins. The attack was found using multiple persistence mechanisms to maintain access. The initial payload creates a scheduled task running every 30 minutes, while the downloader establishes another task to repeatedly execute daily at 1 AM. The Gh0st RAT, meanwhile, adds itself to the Windows registry’s Run key, installs a Windows service and creates a scheduled task that launches it every 30 minutes. Barney said cryptominers may serve as a distraction from the more serious implications of an intrusion. Attackers, he noted, can use mining activity as “a smokescreen for establishing long-term persistence through remote access tools.” FortiGuard said it provides detection coverage for the campaign through its FortiGuard IPS, Web Filtering, and Antivirus services. For those who aren’t its customers, the company shared a list of indicators of compromise (IoCs) to help catch potential infections.

The attackers are using predefined username and password lists to brute-force into these servers and exploit their administrative capabilities to execute commands on the underlying Windows systems. The activity highlights the persistent challenge of securing privileged access across complex and often legacy infrastructure, said Shane Barney , chief information security officer at Keeper Security. “While internet-facing databases are sometimes the unintended result of technical debt or misconfigurations, relying on static, standing credentials is what turns that exposure into a critical vulnerability,” he said.

title: AI found Linux kernel bugs that remained undetected for decades
raw_text: A Microsoft research project combining AI agents with human security researchers uncovered 59 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including bugs that had survived in production code for more than 20 years. While AI dramatically accelerated the discovery process, the researchers found that validating flaws, developing patches, and working with maintainers remained overwhelmingly human-intensive. The research, conducted by Microsoft’s FORGE Lab under the codename MDASH, generated 26,502 potential findings in approximately two weeks of scanning selected Linux kernel subsystems. Automated screening, proof-of-concept testing, and human validation narrowed these down to 59 public upstream reports, Microsoft said in a blog post. “We developed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline,” the researchers said in the blog post. From thousands of findings to 59 reports Microsoft said it scanned selected kernel components covering networking, filesystems, and security modules. The initial findings were reduced to 11,769 candidates through automated screening. AI agents then attempted to reproduce potential vulnerabilities using QEMU, an open-source machine emulator. This produced 621 cases with proof-of-concept evidence. Human researchers reviewed these cases to identify root causes, merge duplicates, and prepare upstream submissions, the blog post added. Of the 621 cases, 59 resulted in public upstream reports. Microsoft said another 266 shared root causes with other findings and could be addressed through the same patch. A further 163 were not reported following review, mostly because of limited security impact, while 133 had already been reported or fixed upstream. Microsoft said its first public report was submitted on June 27, 2026. By September 1, 55 of the 59 reports had been posted to public mailing lists. The remaining four were reported privately during the same period and routed to public lists by mid-October. Of the 33 CVEs assigned to the findings, 24 carry a High or higher severity rating, based on CVSS v3.1 scores of at least 7.0, according to Microsoft. Eight vulnerabilities had working exploits The eight vulnerabilities for which Microsoft developed working local privilege-escalation exploits affect several kernel components, including IPv4 and IPv6 networking, IPsec routing, encrypted-key handling and the resizable hash-table implementation. Some demonstrations required non-default settings or disabled exploit mitigations, the researchers said. One finding, CVE-2026-64563, involves the kernel’s rhashtable implementation, a shared resizable hash-table library used by different kernel subsystems. Microsoft traced the flaw to a 2018 code change that allowed a table-walk operation to retain a pointer when paused. Under specific conditions involving table resizing and the removal of an entry, the kernel could subsequently access freed memory through that stale pointer. The researchers identified an exploitable path through Netlink socket diagnostics, which are accessible to unprivileged users. By manipulating memory, an attacker could turn the flaw into a constrained kernel memory-write primitive that, combined with other exploitation techniques, could enable local privilege escalation, Microsoft explained. The company said this vulnerability was exploitable on standard Linux configurations without requiring special kernel configurations or user namespaces. It also affected Android devices with SELinux enforcing. Across the 59 reports, the average age of a bug was 8.1 years when Microsoft first reported it publicly. One vulnerability, CVE-2026-74544, had been present in the kernel for at least 21 years, the researchers said. Patching remains a lengthy process While AI agents helped identify potential vulnerabilities, generate proof-of-concept demonstrations and draft initial patches, Microsoft said human investigation remained necessary to validate findings and work with Linux kernel maintainers. “Upstream Linux typically requires vulnerability reports to come with a working patch. Agents helped draft initial fixes, but human validation, subsystem understanding, and iterating with maintainers during review remained essential,” the researchers wrote. Fixes for 38 of the 59 reports had been merged into the upstream Linux mainline at the time of publication. Half were accepted with the initial submission, while the others required between one and four revisions. The median time from the first public patch submission to a mainline release was 41 days, with the longest taking 108 days, Microsoft said. Work with maintainers on the remaining reports was continuing. Microsoft said the initial scans took about two weeks, but converting the findings into validated reports and patches required more than four person-months of work. “Finding bugs and fixing them are drastically out of balance,” the researchers wrote. “For complex infrastructure like the Linux kernel, keeping humans in the loop is still necessary, making human effort the bottleneck.” The researchers said the project covered only a small fraction of the Linux kernel and that further tuning of the AI-assisted approach could uncover additional bugs. However, they cautioned that finding more vulnerabilities would not necessarily make systems more secure. “More tokens may yield more bugs, but not a secure system,” the blog post concluded.
summary: A Microsoft research project combining AI agents with human security researchers uncovered 59 Linux kernel vulnerabilities, including bugs that had survived in production code for more than 20 years. While AI dramatically accelerated the discovery process, the researchers found that validating flaws, developing patches, and working with maintainers remained overwhelmingly human-intensive. The research, conducted by Microsoft’s FORGE Lab under the codename MDASH, generated 26,502 potential findings in approximately two weeks of scanning selected Linux kernel subsystems. Automated screening, proof-of-concept testing, and human validation narrowed these down to 59 public upstream reports, Microsoft said in a blog post.

title: The developer laptop just became production. Now what?
raw_text: For decades, enterprise software development relied on an assumption that developers could experiment relatively safely because there were safeguards between their work and production. Development, staging and production had different rules, with human intermediaries making judgments about what was ready to move forward. Testing also assumed that software would behave predictably when executed again. Coding agents are upending both assumptions. Developers now run autonomous software on laptops containing GitHub tokens, SSH keys, cloud credentials and authenticated browser sessions. They’re connecting agents to MCP servers, granting access to repositories and services, and copying suggested commands into terminals without always understanding what those commands will do. When permission prompts become an obstacle, it’s tempting to click through them or enable unrestricted access. Developers are inventing security policies on the fly. The result is that the developer laptop has become an extension of production . An agent can reach systems that previously required deliberate human intervention, often using permissions granted for an entirely different purpose. Unlike conventional software, an agent may take different actions when presented with the same task because its context and decisions change. CISOs now face a fundamentally different challenge: governing autonomous software that already holds active pathways into production. The security control we never recognized was human judgment Where human developers and coding agents diverge most sharply is in judgment, not technical capability. Developers understand what state their code is in, whether it’s something they’re testing or something that’s production-ready. They understand what their credentials permit them to do, but also when and how those credentials should be used. There’s an implicit compartmentalization between having access and exercising it. An AI agent is much more single-minded. If an available credential helps accomplish the task, the agent uses it. Agents don’t recognize the distinction between what is technically possible and what policy permits. Consider an agent asked to troubleshoot a failing application. It discovers production credentials on the developer’s laptop and determines that querying the live database is the fastest way to diagnose the problem. It might modify production data while attempting a fix, even though the developer intended only to investigate a local issue. No vulnerability needs to be exploited. The agent simply uses available authority to pursue its assigned objective. Traditional development pipelines weren’t designed around software that independently decides which systems to access and what actions to take. Security controls must now account for behavior that can’t be fully anticipated from the original request. A sandbox can contain an agent without containing its authority Sandboxing has emerged as an obvious response to the risks of autonomous agents . By isolating execution inside a container, virtual machine or microVM, organizations can limit an agent’s ability to interfere with its host or other workloads. Strong isolation is essential, particularly when agents execute untrusted code or interact with potentially malicious tools. A microVM with its own guest kernel can provide a stronger boundary than a conventional container sharing the host kernel. But isolation answers only part of the security question. An agent sandbox that blocks all external access is as useful as a computer encased in cement at the bottom of the ocean. An agent doesn’t have to escape its sandbox to cause a security incident. It can misuse perfectly legitimate permissions, send sensitive information through an authorized network connection or make destructive changes using credentials deliberately provided to it. Isolating execution is useless unless you also precisely control what that workload can reach. A secure sandbox containing unrestricted credentials still leaves an enormous attack surface. Can you revoke an agent without disabling its developer? Security professionals are familiar with least privilege, but agentic development exposes the limitations of conventional identity and access management. Consider a developer who authorizes an agent to modify one GitHub repository. If the agent uses the developer’s personal token, it may inherit access to every repository that developer can reach . That could include merge permissions, CI/CD environments and downstream credentials associated with those systems. This is ambient authority: the ability to perform actions beyond the particular task for which access was originally intended. Even a relatively narrow token may authorize repeated actions when the agent only needed permission to perform the action once. When an agent operates under a developer’s credentials, revoking its access can also mean disabling the developer. Security teams need to separate autonomous workloads from human identity. Agents should have independently defined identities, with permissions delegated for specific purposes. That makes it possible to track what each agent did, investigate where something went wrong and revoke an individual agent’s authority without disrupting its developer. The missing link is a trusted broker One of the most interesting developments in agentic security is the emerging idea of a trusted broker that sits between an agent and the systems it wants to access. Some approaches are described as MCP proxies. Others use authorization services, gateways or different architectures. What they’re circling is the same fundamental problem: how do we decide which agents can access which resources, under what circumstances and for how long? Crucially, the agent cannot be responsible for deciding the limits of its own authority. Those decisions must be enforced by a separate system that can authorize individual operations without surrendering the credentials that make them possible. Imagine asking an agent to fix a GitHub issue. Instead of granting unrestricted repository access, the developer authorizes the task once. A trusted intermediary could then permit the agent to read the repository, push changes to a designated branch and open a pull request. Those permissions could expire after an hour, without exposing a broadly reusable developer credential. This is the core tension agentic security has to resolve. Grant too little access and developers abandon the controls. Grant too much and isolation becomes irrelevant to the damage an authorized agent can cause. The goal is to make secure delegation as frictionless as unrestricted access. Agentic security may be approaching a comparable architectural moment. Developers, open-source projects and commercial vendors are experimenting with approaches to identity, delegation, authorization and policy enforcement. Some organizations are building their own controls around existing IAM systems. Others are exploring dedicated intermediaries that evaluate requests before allowing agents to reach external resources. The trusted broker is not yet a universally defined component, and there’s no guarantee one implementation will become the equivalent of Kubernetes. Questions about policy decisions, credential custody, latency, availability and auditability remain open. But the missing function is becoming clearer. We need a dependable intermediary that translates human intent into narrowly defined, enforceable authority for autonomous software. MCP servers have become a new software supply chain MCP is one of the principal ways agents connect to external tools and information. That makes it both an important integration mechanism and a security boundary. A malicious MCP server can become an indirect route into an agent’s workflow. If servers or tools execute with access to shared filesystems, processes or credential stores, a compromised component may be able to read secrets belonging to another tool. But credential theft isn’t the only concern. A compromised server can return manipulated information that influences an agent’s subsequent actions even before the agent uses the tool. An attacker doesn’t need to compromise the agent—only the context it consumes. The familiar disciplines of provenance, signing and build integrity need to extend to MCP servers, agent tools and model weights. Organizations should know where these components originated, whether they’ve been modified and what authority they receive when introduced into an environment. The answer is layered security: strong isolation, independently managed identities, narrowly scoped permissions, controlled network access and sufficient observability to understand what agents actually do. Why agent security belongs in the execution path Containerization demonstrated that security works best when guardrails are baked directly into developer platforms without stripping away speed. Kubernetes eventually made it possible to enforce common security and operational policies across distributed workloads without requiring every developer to become an infrastructure expert. Agentic development needs a comparable shift. The longer-term opportunity is to move from granting persistent access to delegating task-specific authority. Developers need a way to authorize an agent to fix one issue or open one pull request without surrendering standing keys. Laptops are production endpoints now, and they won’t revert back to safe sandboxes. Security teams must protect developer speed by embedding the boundaries that human judgment used to handle manually directly into the infrastructure.
summary: For decades, enterprise software development relied on an assumption that developers could experiment relatively safely because there were safeguards between their work and production. Development, staging and production had different rules, with human intermediaries making judgments about what was ready to move forward. Testing also assumed that software would behave predictably when executed again. Coding agents are upending both assumptions.

title: Hackers stole AI credentials to get $740,000 in free compute; Railway picked up the bill
raw_text: As AI model training and distillation increase, AI tokens are becoming a piping hot currency for threat actors. Cloud hosting provider Railway found out the hard way; it has confirmed a near 26-hour battle against attackers targeting AI provider credentials to sell to AI ‘transfer stations’ for use in model distillation. The crooks generated about $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges using the stolen credentials and potentially had access to up to 100,000 workspace credentials. Railway said the attacker’s database searches looked for AI provider keys by name before anything else; some queries also targeted cloud, database, and payment service credentials. The company disclosed the incident on October 22 , and posted a follow-up report this week. Because of the ongoing investigation, it is not able to share the specific details and scale of the exploits, but advised users to revoke and reapply sensitive environmental variables stored on Railway prior to October 21. “AI credentials are becoming the new credit card numbers,” said David Shipley of Beauceron Security. “So-called LLMjacking is expected to displace Cryptojacking as a cheap, scalable way to make money.” A 26-hour battle The attack began on October 20, when hackers exploited a previously unknown vulnerability in Railway’s build infrastructure. They were able to evade filesystem isolation protections and obtain an internal credential that they used to access stored build histories. From there, they retrieved a copy of Railway’s internal source code and analyzed it to identify additional avenues of compromise. They then exploited another vulnerability involving an improperly configured trust relationship that allowed them to gain even more access to Railway’s infrastructure and obtain credentials used to decrypt customer environment variables. In a nearly 26-hour battle, Railway’s engineering team worked 24-7 in shifts and the escalating situation became a “contest of agent speed,” the company explained. The threat actor chained various exploits, moved laterally across multiple systems, and “probed many potential routes, in parallel.” Defenders in turn hardened routes in parallel. “This was not a single breach followed by a single fix,” Railway wrote. The threat actors were “fully evicted” on October 21, but over the course of their time in the system, they obtained and decrypted a “subset” of customer variables, roughly 100,000, or “at most” 1.85% of workspaces. They also racked up $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges, with customers reporting their keys answered coding questions and performed training-data tasks they never ran. The company is working to reimburse customers, including for charges providers decline to refund. The breach also exposed linked-account tokens belonging to more than 1,850 users, which included GitHub and OAuth tokens that Railway says it reset. The company worked quickly with GitHub, GitLab, Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, SpaceXSI, Stripe, and others to revoke potentially compromised keys. In the wake of the attack, customers have been advised to remove public network access to databases; rotate any sensitive variables and keys; check GitHub account audit logs and review all app access; and check audit logs within registries such as Dockerhub. On its own systems, Railway said it shut down any potentially compromised internal tooling; rolled all keys and “then rerolled them” after validating that intruders had been shut out; moved to a new generation of infrastructure; rebuilt tooling used to run its infrastructure; and added functionality to mass revoke Railway app permissions in the event of suspicious activity in the future. Why attackers want AI keys AI credentials are cheap to harvest at scale, Shipley noted; attackers can hit a provider like Railway rather than trying to target one company at a time. That access can then be resold to generate revenue through so-called AI routers, which provide access to models that users otherwise could not afford, or even reach. This makes that access a hot commodity for tasks like d istillation , which transfers knowledge from a larger model to a smaller one to cut costs and improve efficiency. Training one model on another model’s answers at scale takes millions of questions, said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research, and a single account asking millions of questions stands out. Stolen keys spread those questions across thousands of real customers. “Think of copying a textbook one page at a time, using library cards that belong to other people,” Dickson explained. Frontier AI is expensive to buy, and the owner of the keys gets the bill while the thief gets cost-free compute. “It is the 2026 version of cryptomining; [the] same playbook with a different output,” he said. Managing identities when so many are machine-held Even though the facts are ugly, Railway deserves credit for a “remarkably candid report,” Dickson emphasized: It owns its own configuration mistake, it admits it cannot be sure it found every account the attacker created, and it commits to telling customers of issues more quickly in the future. Railway is now moving to short-lived credentials and logging every decryption. That is the right fix, Dickson said, and every platform holding customer secrets should copy it. “Railway customers should treat every secret stored on the platform as stolen until they have rotated it,” he noted. But that rotation has to beat the thief’s clock; an investigation by Wiz found that stolen keys were tested within 30 minutes of theft, then flooded with traffic four to seven days later. Start with AI provider keys, then rotate cloud, database, and payment credentials, he advised. Check AI provider bills and usage logs for traffic internal teams did not generate, then report any unauthorized charges to Railway. Alert on any call from an unrecognized address. Further, he said, limit the damage any one key can do. Set hard spending caps and usage alerts on every AI key, and scope each key as narrowly as the provider allows. This really works: In one case Wiz examined, a key restricted to a narrow set of model profiles left most of the thief’s traffic throttled. Non-Railway users, meanwhile, should ask their platform providers two questions: How are my secrets stored, and who can decrypt them? A good standard practice: Issue fewer keys. “No one ever said during a key rotation that they wished they had issued more keys,” Dickson pointed out. Ultimately, he said, a stolen AI key spends real money, and machines now hold most of the keys. “Protect machine identities like cash, because to a thief, that is exactly what they are,” Dickson urged.

Cloud hosting provider Railway found out the hard way; it has confirmed a near 26-hour battle against attackers targeting AI provider credentials to sell to AI ‘transfer stations’ for use in model distillation. The crooks generated about $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage charges using the stolen credentials and potentially had access to up to 100,000 workspace credentials. title: Microsoft outage: Impact shows risk of M365 bundle lock-in
raw_text:
Several UK government departments, hospitals and schools have said they cannot send or receive email messages due to the global outage of Microsoft Exchange, which has impacted organisations that use Microsoft 365 products.

The Planning Inspectorate’s Manage Appeals Service said it has been temporarily paused for new submissions and customer access due to an email and system problem, and the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency claimed it has been experiencing issues sending and receiving emails, and that it has provided a phone number for urgent queries.

The Maritime and Coastguard Agency also wrote that it was experiencing problems sending and receiving emails due to the worldwide Microsoft outage, but added that its search and rescue services have not been affected.

Police Scotland said: “We are unable to receive any emails, and there may be a delay in responding to any forms sent to us in the last 24 hours as this outage continues.”  

Merseyside police wrote in a post that it had staff on duty 24/7 to answer non-emergency queries on Facebook, X and Instagram. 

The NHS reported that staff were working to ensure critical services and appointments continue for patients, despite the outage. It urged patients to attend appointments as usual unless told otherwise. 

Mersey Care NHS Foundation Trust stated that it was aware of the outage but that teams were still available by phone to manage any urgent referrals. 

Glasgow City Council said it was experiencing disruption to some services, and that schools had texted parents and carers to alert them.  

Walsall Council posted that people might experience intermittent issues accessing council services online or receiving notifications, but that phones were still working.  

The Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea said residents my “find it harder than usual to contact us, and it could take us longer to respond”.

  • CMA investigates ‘free’ Copilot subscription in M365: The regulator is looking at whether the Personal and Family Microsoft 365 subscription lured people into a premium Copilot subscription on renewal.

A number of schools said their email systems were not working and advised parents to contact them by phone or in person, while the UK’s Supreme Court reported that it was not receiving emails, its online contact forms and portal were still functioning as normal.

As Computer Weekly has reported, more than 130,000 users logged problems with Outlook on Downdetector at its peak, demonstrating the economic and human costs of relying heavily on a single technology provider, which has left businesses and public services vulnerable to facing disruption.

There is also a potential cyber risk given that Microsoft security products including Microsoft Defender and Intune have been impacted by the outage, as well as its data protection and IT governance tool, Purview, which provides authorisation, data loss prevention and role-based access.

Even as some services become available, the job for IT admins is only just starting due to service degradation affecting Microsoft cyber security, data protection and compliance tools, which means hackers have had a window of opportunity to target organisations impacted by the outage.

Marie Wilcox, vice-president of market strategy at Binalyze, said: “The wisest approach is for security teams to treat the outage window as an incident in its own right. That means going back over sign-ins, mailbox rules, account changes and endpoint activity from the hours when visibility dropped, and collecting evidence directly from devices rather than relying on the platform that was down. Most will find nothing. But ‘probably nothing’ isn’t an answer a board, regulator or insurer will accept, and it’s exactly the assumption attackers count on.”

title: Government investigation into Post Office system too late for appeal against conviction
raw_text:
A government investigation into pre-Horizon systems used in Post Office branches will come too late for inclusion in a former subpostmaster’s appeal against a conviction based on one of the systems in the spotlight.

The Department for Business and Trade recently announced its planned investigation into systems used by subpostmasters before the controversial Horizon software at the centre of the Post Office scandal.

The government is yet to appoint a company to carry out the investigation and will not report until spring next year. But the appeal against the conviction of former subpostmasters Gareth Snow, in January, which Post Office is contesting, will cover the reliability of the Payment Service (APS) and Automatic Payment Terminal (APT) system. It has been confirmed that APT/APS are “among the systems the department intends the investigation to cover, alongside ECCO+, ALPS and ESNS”.

Cart before the horse

The subpostmaster’s legal team is seeking more information. Solicitor Neil Hudgell at Hudgell Solicitors, which represents Snow, said: “We welcome the review, but need to know more before we determine to what extent it impacts the progression of Mr Snow’s appeal.”

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), which referred the appeal, has already said that the system which Snow used in his branch in Denbighshire “could cause accounting errors”.

Computer Weekly put to the government that the APT/APS appeal comes before the investigation and a spokesperson replied: “We are committed to getting to the truth about the impact of systems used before Horizon and continue to make progress towards appointing an independent investigator. We expect to confirm further details shortly.”

APT/APS is lesser known that Horizon and Capture, but was used by thousands of branches. In a 1994 news article in the Barry and District News, Richard Dykes, then managing director at Post Office Counters, was quoted as saying the APT/APS system was already installed in 3,000 Post Office branches, with the aim of reaching 6,000 over the following 12 months. It included an electronic terminal connected to telephone lines and was used to carry out transactions such as rent, rates and utility payments.

If Snow’s appeal is heard prior to the investigation report, it will not be based on a full picture, according to investigative scientist Ian Ross, a listed expert for the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague.

“Deciding an appeal weeks before a major state report on the exact same software is a psychological trap for the court,” he said. “Without the complete findings on APS/APT, judges are left anchoring their decisions to incomplete data – risking a verdict shaped by what is missing rather than what is true.”

Pre-Horizon problems

There are currently four former subpostmasters with appeals, due to be heard in the Court of Appeal, which blame systems that came before Fujitsu’s Horizon system for the unexplained losses they were blamed for.

The other three were Capture users, a pre-Horizon system that has already been investigated and found there was a “reasonable likelihood” it caused accounting losses. The Post Office is also contesting these.

Read Computer Weekly’s investigation of bug from 2015: Post Office IT support email reveals known Horizon flaw.

Snow’s appeal is due to be heard alongside the posthumous appeal former Capture users Patricia Owen, who died in 2003; and Steve Marston, a who ran a Post Office branch in Bury, Lancashire.

The focus on systems used before Horizon has become necessary due to a huge body of evidence highlighting the Post Office’s treatment of unexplained shortfalls as the fuel behind the scandal. The arm’s length government body made subpostmasters take responsibility for unexplained shortfalls and kept quiet about its knowledge of bugs in the system that could cause discrepancies.

During a select committee hearing in January, the CCRC told MPs that there are 35 applications of interest, which it refers to as “pre-Horizon”. It said that any of these systems could be linked to miscarriages of justice, and it is not a giant leap to suggest that pre-Horizon software also caused unexplained shortfalls that subpostmasters were forced to cover.

There are 12 pre-Horizon cases currently being reviewed by the CCRC. A total of 40 pre-Horizon applications have been received in total, with 21 not referred to appeal, two withdrawn and four have already been referred. There was also a case that turned out to be related to Horizon and so was covered by legislation to overturn convictions.

summary:
A government investigation into pre-Horizon systems used in Post Office branches will come too late for inclusion in a former subpostmaster’s appeal against a conviction based on one of the systems in the spotlight.

The Department for Business and Trade recently announced its planned investigation into systems used by subpostmasters before the controversial Horizon software at the centre of the Post Office scandal.

The government is yet to appoint a company to carry out the investigation and will not report until spring next year. But the appeal against the conviction of former subpostmasters Gareth Snow, in January, which Post Office is contesting, will cover the reliability of the Payment Service (APS) and Automatic Payment Terminal (APT) system. It has been confirmed that APT/APS are “among the systems the department intends the investigation to cover, alongside ECCO+, ALPS and ESNS”.

Cart before the horse

The subpostmaster’s legal team is seeking more information. Solicitor Neil Hudgell at Hudgell Solicitors, which represents Snow, said: “We welcome the review, but need to know more before we determine to what extent it impacts the progression of Mr Snow’s appeal.”

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), which referred the appeal, has already said that the system which Snow used in his branch in Denbighshire “could cause accounting errors”.

Computer Weekly put to the government that the APT/APS appeal comes before the investigation and a spokesperson replied: “We are committed to getting to the truth about the impact of systems used before Horizon and continue to make progress towards appointing an independent investigator.

title: Global Microsoft outage leaves users open to phishing attacks
raw_text:
Microsoft users globally have been unable to access services such as Outlook and Teams due to technical issues, which the company has described as “service degradation”.

The Microsoft Cloud status portal says users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 services. The degradation of service impacts Exchange Online, Microsoft 365 Admin Center, Microsoft 365 applications, CoPilot 365, Microsoft Fabric, Defender, and Defender XDR and Microsoft Intune.

While most of the core functionality in Teams is unaffected, Microsoft warned that anything that relies on features like the Exchange Online calendar to schedule meetings is potentially impacted. 

For applications such as Power Apps, Microsoft said affected users may be able to use Power Apps or Field Service on the web as a way to circumvent impact. It also stated that users who are already signed in can potentially avoid impact by not signing out, clearing app data or reinstalling the software.

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid suspected spy affair scandal
raw_text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned from his post after coming under fire over a series of extramarital affairs, with the company’s stock tanking when the US markets opened on Thursday morning.

One of the women in question, named as Alice Huang, was linked to Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, but the US government has said she may have been in the pay of China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency, allegedly tasked with helping Chinese organisations obtain advanced Nvidia chipsets in defiance of US export controls.

Huang had been vocal in his desire to export artificial intelligence (AI) chips to China more broadly, and had been lobbying US president Donald Trump extensively – he notably committed $25m to Trump’s controversial ballroom project, alongside other tech firms including Apple, Google and Meta.

In an email to staff obtained by CNBC, Huang said: “I owe my family and all of you an apology. I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.

“Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, Nvidia’s board of directors has initiated an independent investigation,” he added. “I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.”

In a statement, Nvidia said Huang’s impact had been profound, making it one of the “most consequential” tech companies in the world, and thanked him for his “immeasurable contributions” to Nvidia and the industry.

Interim CEO

The organisation moved swiftly to name executive vice-president and chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO until the appointment of a permanent successor.

Kress joined Nvidia in 2013, prior to which she worked in finance roles at Cisco and Microsoft, among others.

“Colette has helped lead Nvidia through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position,” said Harvey Jones, newly appointed chair of the Nvidia board of directors.

“She is supported by an experienced leadership team that has been instrumental in executing Nvidia’s strategy and advancing its technology roadmap,” he continued. “The board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company’s operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.”  

Kress added: “Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.

“We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI and execute on the opportunities ahead,” she said. “Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders.”

Famed for his trademark leather jackets, Huang was born in Taiwan but was sent to live in the US in 1973 as a child, where he became involved in his high school computer club and learned to code on an Apple II.

title: AI & cybersecurity: A Computer Weekly Downtime Upload podcast
raw_text:
Given the ingenuity of AI (artificial intelligence) to power all manner of cyber attack, IT leaders need to consider whether current cybersecurity training is sufficient. Speaking to Computer Weekly during the Gartner Symposium in Barcelona, Akif Khan, a senior director at Gartner, would not be drawn on whether he feels current cyber security education is out-of-date, but he says secure behaviour management needs to evolve beyond protecting organisations from attacks based on phishing.

He says: “When we think about the interfaces that employees have now within chat applications, within phone, video call, e-mail, it's much more of a multimedia environment in which attackers can potentially contact employees.”

As an  example he warns that employees can experience deepfakes within calls or video calls where people are impersonating executives, and try to trick those employees. 

“At the moment, a very common attack is one in which employees receive calls claiming to be from their IT service desk,” he adds.

This is leading providers of IT security training to evolve their courses. For instance, as Khan notes: “Cyber security training vendors now provide training that’s much more tailored towards the deepfake threat.

“With your consent, they will create a deepfake of your executives and use that in the training provided to employees. They use AI agents in the training such that an employee receives a phishing phone call in which the agent is having a conversation with them, trying to get them to reveal sensitive information.”

While this demonstrates how employee cybersecurity training is evolving, Khan says: “Most organisations are now behind the curve in terms of actually utilising this more forward-looking form of training.” 

Along with user training, there is an on-going discussion over how to secure agentic AI systems. Assuming AI agents do not simply adopt user credentials and are not treated merely as digital employees, Khan believes agentic AI security does not really fall within the scope of what would impact typical employee awareness training. 

Khan has been speaking at the Gartner conference about  identity and access management and how that applies to agentic AI.  He says: “What most of our clients are interested in right now is how you can manage identity and access management for AI agents. This is crucial.  It's important that first of all AI agents are each given their own unique identity.  They should never inherit the identity of the human that created them because they are separate entities.”

As an example, using an AI agent to submit expenses on someone’s behalf, which will save the user the time to do this task, will require the agent to have his own unique identity. Khan says it should only be authorised to use the corporate IT systems that enable it to access the expenses application. “And when the agent accesses the expense application, it should only be authorised to carry out, for example, submitting an expense.”

With identity and access management, the identity of the agent is ephemeral so the credentials to access the expense application are temporary. “By locking down enterprise IT, you've implemented identity and access management correctly and in a way that prevents the agent accessing another system,” Khan adds. “It prevents the agent from doing something it shouldn't be doing within the expenses system and essentially provides  a clear audit trail with human accountability as to what that agent does.”
