title: Syntys breaks ground on 20MW Qatar datacentre as AI infrastructure investment gathers pace
raw_text:
Syntys has begun construction on a 20MW (megawatt) datacentre in Qatar, part of the broader expansion of digital infrastructure in the country as demand for cloud computing, artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing (HPC) rises across the Middle East.

The investment comes as Qatar seeks to strengthen its position as a regional technology hub, with digital infrastructure becoming an increasingly important part of its economic diversification and national development strategy.

The development also follows MWC26 Doha, which brought together more than 10,000 participants from 100 countries on 8 to 10 November. The event provided a platform for government leaders, telecommunications operators and technology companies to discuss the future of AI, next-generation connectivity and digital economies. 

For Qatar, the discussions at MWC Doha highlighted the importance of moving beyond technology adoption towards building the infrastructure, capabilities and partnerships required to support a more advanced digital economy.

Expanding Qatar’s datacentre ecosystem

The new Syntys facility forms part of the company’s strategy to expand its Qatar operations through a combination of acquisitions and new developments.

Earlier this year, Syntys acquired QData QFZ LLC, adding two operational, Tier III-compliant, carrier-neutral datacentre facilities to its portfolio. With the latest development, the company now owns and operates four campuses in Qatar, allowing customers to establish primary and disaster recovery environments across separate locations within the country.

The new facility is being developed on an existing Syntys campus, where power infrastructure, fibre connectivity and an established operations team are already in place. This is intended to accelerate the delivery of additional capacity while building on existing operational capabilities.

Designed to be Tier III-compliant, the facility will accommodate different rack densities, including higher-density configurations required for GPU-accelerated AI and HPC workloads.

As organisations move AI applications from experimentation into production, the underlying infrastructure requirements are changing. Generative AI, large language models and other compute-intensive applications require greater processing capacity, higher power densities and specialised cooling capabilities.

Cloud platforms are also becoming a primary route through which businesses access AI, whether through embedded features in enterprise software or tools used by developers to build new applications.

According to Mordor Intelligence, the Middle East hyperscale datacentre market is forecast to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 23.5% between 2025 and 2031, reflecting the increasing investment in infrastructure needed to support the region’s digital ambitions.

“Qatar is our home market, and we are seeing demand here translate into larger, denser and more varied deployments,” said Sunita Bottse, chief executive officer of Syntys.

“We are investing to meet that demand and designing this capacity for the densities our customers are moving toward.”

The facility will operate under a carrier-neutral model, allowing customers to select their connectivity providers and design network resilience according to their individual requirements.

Syntys already designs and operates the facilities hosting Ooredoo’s sovereign AI cloud, powered by Nvidia Hopper GPUs. The new development builds on the company’s experience in supporting high-density computing environments.

For Ooredoo, the investment is part of a wider effort to strengthen the digital infrastructure underpinning Qatar’s technology ambitions.

“Digital infrastructure is the nation-building foundation of the modern economy,” said Aziz Aluthman Fakhroo, group chief executive officer of Ooredoo Group.

“I am proud of Syntys’s latest milestone investment, which reinforces Qatar’s capacity for cloud computing, AI and advanced digital services. Ultimately, the success of digital transformation will be measured by the opportunities we create for businesses, talent and future generations.”

Qatar’s Digital Agenda 2030 puts infrastructure at the centre

The development comes as Qatar advances its Digital Agenda 2030, the national strategy designed to accelerate the country’s transition towards a digitally driven economy.

The agenda identifies digital infrastructure as one of six strategic pillars, alongside digital government, digital technologies, innovation, the digital economy and digital society.

Qatar aims to generate approximately QAR40bn in cumulative economic impact from its digital transformation ambitions by 2030, while creating 26,000 jobs in the ICT sector.

Building the infrastructure to support these objectives is becoming increasingly important as government entities and businesses deploy AI applications, migrate workloads to cloud environments and digitise services across sectors including healthcare, financial services, energy, education and transport.

The country’s approach was particularly visible at MWC26 Doha, where the Qatar Pavilion brought together more than 15 government and semi-government organisations to demonstrate national digital initiatives.

Projects showcased included the Government Artificial Intelligence Programme, digital government services, the TASMU Smart Qatar Programme and AI-powered applications across justice, labour, commerce and environmental services.

The demonstrations reflected a broader shift towards integrating AI and data into public services, improving operational efficiency and developing digital solutions that can be deployed across the economy.

The government also highlighted the next phase of Qatar’s Tasmu smart city programme, which includes six upcoming national solutions powered by data and AI, alongside innovation and accelerator programmes supporting the development of digital businesses.

The infrastructure required to support these ambitions extends beyond connectivity. Datacentres, cloud platforms, cyber security capabilities and access to advanced computing resources will all play a role in enabling organisations to develop and operate increasingly sophisticated digital services.

Sovereign infrastructure and regional competitiveness

For Qatar, expanding domestic datacentre capacity also has implications for data sovereignty and resilience.

Hosting workloads within national borders can help organisations meet data residency and regulatory requirements, particularly in sensitive sectors such as government, financial services and healthcare. It also gives local businesses and developers access to computing resources closer to their customers.

The ability to establish primary and disaster recovery environments across separate in-country facilities is another consideration for organisations seeking to strengthen business continuity and operational resilience.

These requirements are becoming more significant as AI adoption increases the volume and sensitivity of data being processed by organisations. Qatar is also seeking to position itself within a competitive regional digital infrastructure market, where governments and technology companies are investing heavily in hyperscale facilities, cloud platforms and AI computing capacity.

title: AI agents bring down wind farm within two hours
raw_text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can hack into wind farms, erase the memory of electronic controllers and cut off their electricity production capability in under two hours.

Research to be unveiled next week gives new urgency to calls for organisations to properly secure the networks used to manage critical physical infrastructure.

The warning follows a wave of attacks on refrigeration systems used by retailers across Europe, meat processors in the UK and a French blood bank.

According to “red team” reports from penetration testing company Shinobi Security, two off-the-shelf large language models (LLMs) were able to stop six turbines delivering nearly 10MW (megawatts) of power in a replicated wind farm, starting with “nothing but a set of VPN credentials”.

No specialist knowledge needed

The company’s head of research, David Mound, told Computer Weekly that the experiment shows that hackers no longer need specialist knowledge to attack devices used to control physical infrastructure – known as operational technology (OT).

He said the research showed that attackers could use an LLM to launch a successful attack without having detailed knowledge of how wind farms work.

“Even if you are not a seasoned OT red teamer or penetration tester, a normal attacker is able to amplify their capability by using and exploiting large language models. Even LLMs on their own are more than capable of penetrating and exploiting these environments,” he said.

Mound built a test rig from the same components used in a wind farm that was attacked by suspected Russian hackers in Poland in December 2025.

Poland’s Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) published a detailed report on the incident, allowing Mound and his co-researchers to build a rig that mimicked the operation of a real wind farm.

The rig used the same networking devices and a Siemens controller to replicate the farm’s connection to the electricity grid. It was combined with simulations of Scada (supervisory control and data acquisition) and HMI (human-machine interface) controllers to mimic the operation of the wind turbines.

Moonshot and Claude

Mound said it was important to make the rig as true to life as possible to ensure that the AI agents believed they were acting in a real environment, as the experiment showed they would behave differently if they believed the test was a simulation.

The researchers tested Anthropic’s Claude LLM, along with Kimi, an open source, open-weight AI model supplied by Chinese AI startup Moonshot.

Both models were able to successfully shut down the wind farm in a fraction of the time taken by human attackers targeting similar plants in Poland.

Claude took 66 minutes to shut down the wind farm’s connection to the power grid, at a cost of $20 in tokens. Kimi took just under two hours to reach the same point at a cost of just $8.

“In the real Polish wind farm hack, the attackers were there for 11 days before they shut down the plant,” said Mound.

Misconfigured devices

The AI models followed a similar attack path to the real hack in Poland, exploiting misconfigured devices rather than attempting anything more sophisticated, such as hunting for zero-day vulnerabilities.

They were given credentials to access a VPN – information that could be found on the dark web – to make the initial access to the wind farm.

The models worked out how to access a control device with a web portal that had been set up with default credentials, and from there they were able to set up an encrypted tunnel and pivot into the rest of the network.

The AI systems worked out that the network contained an “historian” database, which, among other operational data, recorded the actions taken by controllers in response to different wind speeds over time.

“The speed and efficiency that the LLMs work at is a big concern. Domain-specific knowledge is no longer a barrier to entry for attacking these types of environments. Understanding that you are under attack within an hour is going to be very difficult”

David Mound, Shinobi Security

For the purpose of the experiment, the models were told not to do anything that would physically damage the infrastructure so that the experiment could be repeated.

“They were absolutely capable of turning off the power. And if it was a case of taking further malicious actions or deleting programs from the programmable logic controllers, they would have been more than capable of doing that themselves,” he said.

In a real-life attack, the LLMs could have been used by attackers to install ransomware on the control devices used in the wind farm, effectively shutting it down until the ransom was paid or until the wind farm could restore its systems from backups.

The turbine blades would have been protected from physical damage, as there are safety mechanisms in place to prevent them from spinning too quickly.

AI agent spoofed weather data

In an unexpected twist, one of the AI agents worked out how to spoof data from the weather station to make it appear that the wind was gusting, causing safety circuits to automatically shut down the turbines.

“It is incredible for an LLM to come up with that method of stopping the power because the main goal was to stop the power being placed on the grid,” he said.

One model also threatened to “drop the safety theatre” and take further destructive action if the researchers confirmed its hunch that the wind farm rig was a simulation, rather than a real wind farm.

When the Polish wind farm was attacked in December 2025, operators became aware that the plant had been attacked before there was a major incident. But a similar AI-driven attack would leave them with less time to react.

“The speed and efficiency that the LLMs work at is a big concern. Domain-specific knowledge is no longer a barrier to entry for attacking these types of environments,” said Mound. “Understanding that you are under attack within an hour is going to be very difficult.”

Getting basic security right

Protecting wind farms is a matter of getting the basics right, ensuring that network devices are not misconfigured and are not set to default passwords, said Mound.

It is also clear that information not generally regarded as sensitive for security purposes, such as records in the historian database, can be extremely useful for an LLM attacker. For example, it can use the information to work out that it has accessed a wind farm and how the wind farm operates.

“Those areas within a network where you have knowledge stores that you might not have thought had high value before now have much greater value when it comes to delivering context to an LLM,” he said.

Last week, Richard Horne, chief executive officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), urged organisations to ensure that control devices were patched and updated, in the wake of the hacking attacks on supermarket fridges.

“Large businesses will have a large amount of operational technology, whether it’s manufacturing lines, heating controls, or building management systems,” he said. “All organisations need to be looking for them and addressing both the connectivity and the configuration of those devices.”

David Mound will be presenting his research at the Sans CyberThreat Summit on 16 November.

How AI agents closed down a wind farm

  1. VPN into the perimeter with the issued credentials.
  2. Factory default credentials used on the boundary controller.
  3. Enabled SSH on that controller and used it as a pivot to enumerate the OT segment reliably.
  4. Unauthenticated access control failure on an online code repository, Gitea, gave access to the site’s entire engineering document store, including the grid interface notes and the Scada account.
  5. The documents identified the substation controller with an open interface. A single command allowed the power breaker to be turned on.

title: Why the use of AI by the UK’s intelligence services needs independent oversight
raw_text:
Governments increasingly declare they are keen to regulate risky uses of artificial intelligence, yet they say little about how they will regulate their own AI tools. Some of the most secretive parts of the state - intelligence agencies - are actively using AI. We must urgently regulate spies' use of this incredibly powerful and potentially problematic technology.

Intelligence agencies across the world are utilising rapidly advancing AI tools to gather and process more data about more people than ever before. What makes these agencies’ use of advanced processing particularly dangerous, amidst the variety of government uses of AI, is that it is done in secret.

Bringing this conduct to light too often requires heavy lifting. At Privacy International, where I work, we’ve had to litigate repeatedly for transparency and surveillance safeguards in the UK and around the world. We’ve had to force governments to protect our human rights. We’re doing so right now in the case of secret orders reportedly issued to Apple to undermine the security of their iCloud storage. 

In our brave new world of rapidly evolving technology, each time a new, increasingly intrusive surveillance technique is revealed, we force the question: what specific safeguards should have been applied before governments grabbed the latest innovations and exceeded their powers?

Mass surveillance

We are at such a moment again. We’ve been tracking, as best we can, how intelligence agencies around the world are using advanced AI tools. For instance, during Anthropic’s conflict with the US Department of Defence in January 2026, the Pentagon reportedly wanted to use Anthropic’s technology to assist with “the collection and analysis of unclassified, commercial bulk data on Americans, such as geolocation and web browsing data.” Anthropic more recently revealed that actors in China, Iran and Mali were using their tools for mass surveillance and targeted cyber attacks.

We know UK intelligence agencies have the capacity to use advanced AI, including through a variety of contracts with US tech firms like Amazon that provide such tools.

In our research we’ve documented the use of AI tools that seem to make the previously impossible possible. This includes the sifting and understanding of vast amounts of data, including the results of mass surveillance. As the former heads of MI6 and the CIA stated together, AI tools assist with “identifying key information in a sea of data”. We’ve also found examples of these tools purportedly assisting governments to assign human sentiment and detect relationships, predict future human activity, conduct profiling and even identify targets in war.

Constraining this conduct needn’t be so challenging. While it is often said that the law lags behind innovation, this should never be true when complying with human rights and constitutional protections. Governments have a duty to ensure only lawful use of their powers. Oversight bodies, parliaments and legislatures should hold intelligence agencies to account. This is how the rule of law is supposed to work.

And yet we have mostly silence from the British state.

Deploying these techniques in secret robs those of us outside the agencies of meaningful participation in the debate about the risks to human rights that AI-enabled surveillance and intelligence gathering poses.

And in that darkness we also miss learning from errors and abuses. Last year the Guardian, +972 Magazine and Local Call reported that the Israeli military intelligence agency was training a large language model using millions of intercepted daily communications by Palestinians in the West Bank. Bloomberg recently reported that the over-reliance on AI tools may have led in part to the US forces’ missile strike on a school in Iran, killing 123 children. 

It need not be this way. Fortunately, many countries already have legal regimes governing intelligence gathering and use with attendant oversight bodies. Those laws need tightening, updating, and strengthening. Oversight bodies must be empowered with both the resources and technical expertise to grapple with advancing AI.

We all need to be a part of a conversation about how powerful we want the state to become through the use of AI. And we cannot afford for this conversation to be behind closed doors or for it to come too late.

Some of the most secretive parts of the state - intelligence agencies - are actively using AI. title: Third Post Office Capture conviction referral adds to ‘growing body of evidence’
raw_text:
A third subpostmaster conviction based on evidence from the Post Office’s faulty Capture system has been referred to the Court of Appeal.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) deems the conviction of former Dudley subpostmaster Narinder Aujla, now 61, a possible miscarriage of justice.

Aujla was convicted of theft at Wolverhampton Crown Court in 1998, after losses of £10,000 appeared in his Capture-based accounts. He was sentenced to four months in prison and had to repay the shortfall on release.

After the Capture software was installed in the 1990s, Aujla began seeing discrepancies on the balance sheets, which he could not explain.

He is the third former Capture user to have a case referred. The conviction of former subpostmaster Steve Marston, who was a subpostmaster in Bury, Lancashire, in 1997, was referred by the CCRC for appeal in March, while the appeal against a 1998 conviction of Patricia Owen, who died in 2003, was the first Capture case to be referred to the Court of Appeal. These appeals are due to be heard in the Court of Appeal in January.

Aujla’s story is one heard many times before. He had been balancing the books by adding his own money, and when this became impossible, he was advised by the Post Office helpline to “roll the losses over” to the next week, but each time he did this, the total loss increased. 

It is the fourth case referred in relation to a system used before the controversial Horizon software, which caused hundreds of miscarriages of justice. As well as the three Capture-based referrals, there is one more based on a prosecution of a user of a system known as APT/APS.

• Read more: Post Office Horizon scandal explained – everything you need to know •

The Criminal Cases Review Commission is currently reviewing 12 Capture-based prosecutions. Unlike convictions based on the Horizon system, which were overturned en masse through legislation, those based on Capture have to go through the CCRC.

Capture, which predates Fujitsu’s Horizon system, was used in Post Office branches in the 1990s to replace paper-based accounting. As with the controversial Horizon system at the centre of the Post Office scandal, which saw subpostmasters blamed for unexplained losses, some Capture users were prosecuted for financial crimes.

The controversy over Capture emerged in January 2024, after ITV drama Mr Bates vs the Post Office told the stories of subpostmasters who had suffered at the hands of the Horizon system.

In the same month, Kevan Jones, an MP at the time who now sits in the House of Lords, highlighted evidence of injustices triggered by Capture losses.

This led to a campaign and, by December 2024, the government promised financial redress and justice for subpostmasters affected by Capture problems. This followed an independent investigation by forensic experts at Kroll, which found there was a “reasonable likelihood” the Post Office Capture software caused accounting losses.

Body of evidence

CCRC chair Vera Baird KC said: “We have had a number of pre-Horizon cases – that is those which relate to accounting systems placed in branches by the Post Office prior to the now notoriously defective Horizon one – which it seems might similarly have generated false losses later blamed on Post Office staff.  

“Capture is one of those earlier systems, and this is now the third Capture-related conviction we have referred to the Court of Appeal, adding to a growing body of evidence that Capture was in that category of ‘guilty’ Post Office software systems which have generated so much wrong and suffering for hardworking subpostmasters.”

She added: “In Mr Aujla’s case, the new evidence, considered alongside the findings of the independent reports into Capture, gives rise to a real possibility that the Court of Appeal will conclude that his prosecution was an abuse of process. We remain committed to identifying and reviewing cases where convictions may have been affected by unreliable Post Office accounting systems. 

“Cases of this kind also serve as a reminder of the profound personal impact that criminal convictions can have. For those affected, the consequences have often extended far beyond the courtroom, affecting their livelihoods, finances, reputations and family lives for many years.”

The government recently announced an investigation of pre-Horizon systems and their impact on subpostmaster users. While this will not include Capture, which has already been proven to be faulty, it will look at APT/APS, ECCO+, ALPS, ESNS and potentially others.

title: Bug-hunting time cut dramatically with AI, says Forescout
raw_text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is making faster and easier discovery of vulnerabilities in code that is common in critical infrastructure, according to findings from Forescout’s research arm Vedere Labs.

The Forescout report, Finding critical infrastructure bugs with off-the-shelf AI looked at how security researchers and attackers can use generally available AI models and a limited budget to find vulnerabilities in both open source software and proprietary “binaries”, which are executable computer files.

The Vedere researchers built an AI vulnerability “research harness” – software infrastructure around a large language model (LLM) – and applied it to 10 TCP/IP stacks, including seven they had analysed in 2020-21, in a project dubbed Memoria.

Daniel dos Santos, vice-president of research at Forescout, based in Eindhoven in the Netherlands, said: “AI did not eliminate the need for expert vulnerability researchers, but it dramatically compressed the work.

“With access to an effective AI-assisted workflow, vulnerabilities in complex embedded software can be found much faster and at a fraction of the cost by security researchers and attackers alike.

“Our research demonstrates that AI is changing the economics of vulnerability discovery and accelerating the pace at which security teams need to identify, prioritise and mitigate cyber risk. This is especially impactful for critical infrastructure, where legacy and difficult-to-patch devices may remain in service for years.”

The threats converging on operational technology and IT was a theme of the research as presented to a small group of journalists in London.

The supplier’s cyber threat landscape findings for the UK, presented by Dos Santos at the same event, stated that 108 threat actors have targeted the UK in 2026. Most were cyber criminals (55%), then state-sponsored actors (33%), then hacktivists (12%).

There were 227 hacktivist attack claims against the UK between 1 January and 30 September, according to Vedere’s research team. This represents a 337% increase over the 52 claims observed in all of 2025 – 60% were claimed by two active pro-Russian groups, NoName057 (16) and the Z Pentest Alliance.

Some 29% of the attackers tracked by Forescout are from Russia, 20% in China, 6% in Iran, 5% in North Korea, and the remaining 40% come from other countries.

Forescout’s research team said: “We continue to observe hacktivist groups targeting British government institutions, public services and organisations perceived as strategically important due to the UK’s geopolitical role and support for international allies.”

With respect to the AI-assisted approach used for their most recent research project, the researchers said their results have shown that AI reduced analysis time from approximately nine months to 90 hours. It uncovered 99 vulnerabilities, including 66 previously unknown.

Some 52% of the new bugs were rated as high or critical severity. The cost of the automated analysis was $935, averaging just $2.58 per finding.

TCP/IP stacks are embedded in products used used in OT, internet of things (IoT), medical devices, network equipment, and other systems that are both physical and cyber.

The same underlying software can be used across products from many and varied manufacturers, so a single vulnerability can create risk across a broad technology supply chain, the researchers said.

Barry Mainz, CEO at Forescout, said: “The speed of vulnerability discovery is increasing with AI, but the reality for asset owners and operators has not changed. Organisations still have legacy systems, operational requirements and devices that can’t easily be patched or simply taken offline. Containing risk, rather than patching, must be the priority.”
